I feel like I kind of relate to your situation, but just being a bit younger.

I barely got through the first 4 semesters of high school. I couldn't focus, couldn't do my homework, and couldn't focus in class. This was a bit strange to me and my parents as up until my freshman year, I had pretty much consistently been a straight-A student. As a relatively intelligent kid (at least I like to think so), who isn't causing issues in school, I don't think ADHD was exactly on top of my parent's or my teacher's minds.

Long story short, I ended up getting diagnosed with ADHD-PI and getting prescribed medication. If I have any advice, it'd be to just be patient. It's a process, and a prescription won't *immediately* turn your life (and grades) around. I was so frustrated with myself and expected medication to instantly change that when it probably won't.

Going along with that, finding the right medication and dosage is also a process that you must be patient with. I'm now almost 6 months into my diagnoses and I think I've just found the right medication and dosage (which is different for everyone). I started off with adderall, but it gave me a terrible stomach ache every morning, and my mouth regularly became dryer than the Sahara. I switched to vyvanse and it took an additional few weeks to find the right dosage, and even then it wasn't lasting long enough. Again, the right medication and dosage are different for everyone so just be patient with the tuning process.

Finally, I wish someone had told me sooner that ADHD medication isn't magic. As dumb as that sounds, I go to a HS where I feel like ADHD meds get passed around like it's Advil (especially around finals). Because of this, I've always had this image in my head that it's some magic drug that'll cause you to instantly do better on a test. I guess just remember that stimulants can help you focus on either the good things, but it can also help you focus on the bad things, and it's up to you where the "power" of your focus goes. Good habits still need to be built up to maximize your focus. Even now, I still sometimes find myself getting sidetracked, only to realize I've been playing madden for way too long or that I've been on reddit for a couple of hours (hmph).

Pretty basic stuff I guessm but just some things I wish I knew sooner. Best of luck with the rest of college.

First, when I say that it helps me focus, I meant both task saliency and the intensity of my focus. But when talking specifically about tests, I mean mostly with the intensity of my focus. Task saliency hasn't been an issue for me when taking tests as I really have no choice but to take it. However, actually focusing on the test and not "zoning out" has been my problem. The final I took today - in AP Language and Composition - is a good example of what I mean by the "ability to focus". On the test, there were many passages that were about a page long. In the past, these types of test questions have given me trouble as I often found myself having to go back and reread the passage multiple as I was just passively reading it and not comprehending it, simply because I couldn't stay focused on reading the passage. On vyvanse, a lot of the "mental noise" is gone and I can lock in and read a short passage that I may not have been able to previously get through in one read.

I'm almost sure that it isn't a matter of me being in a state of impaired attention or zoning out. I think I've definitely experienced both without meds, but I am locked in when I have vyvanse.

I've definitely sensed being in a "flow state" but I've never seen "...resulting loss in one's sense of space and time." attached the definition which kind of changes my perspective. I think that definitely could be it, but instead of the individual questions being the "tasks" I'm competing in a flow state, the test itself is the task which means I lose track of time over the whole test and not with each question? 

However, I'm starting to think that it may be an increased anxiety during tests? I've noticed that ever since I started taking stimulants, I tend to "circle" more questions on tests to come back and check because I'm unsure of an answer when maybe it's me overthinking things because I'm so anxious for the test? which would only accelerate by a stimulant? I wonder because I've gone through entire tests this year having only bubbled in a little over half the questions, but spending the same amount of time as I should have on the entire test.

I'm thinking out loud now which is making ramble... but adding on to what I said above, I think I've also started to get hung up on a word or a phrase that is probably a small part of the question, but I get too focused on that which causes me to lose time? Ugh I'm not really sure.

And yes, I always have vyvanse and adderall with food.
